questions.prompt: In the exercise, simple RAG with k=3 said the notes did not contain the answer, though the notes were in the folder. What happened?
questions.explain: The run log that links Heron's samples to pipeline 2.3 ranked fourth, so it was never pasted into the prompt. The model can only use what retrieval hands it.

options.text: Retrieval left out the run log, so the link never reached the model
The chat model was too small to read twelve short notes at once
options.misconception: The same model answered correctly when given k=5 or all the notes, so it could read them. The difference was which notes arrived.

options.text: Ollama deleted some notes from the index to save memory
options.misconception: Nothing is deleted. The index is rebuilt in memory on every run and ranks all twelve notes.

options.text: The embedding model cannot handle names such as Heron
options.misconception: Embeddings handle names. The right notes simply scored lower than three other notes for this question.

questions.prompt: Sort each cost or risk by where it shows up in the exercise.
questions.explain: Simple RAG can miss a chunk at retrieval time. A graph adds a build step with an LLM, and the facts it extracts can be wrong.

items.text: The right note ranks below the top k and never reaches the prompt
items.misconception: This is the retrieval miss seen at k=3. The graph walk follows links instead of ranking whole notes.

items.text: A minute and twenty seconds to extract facts from twelve short notes
items.misconception: Embedding twelve notes for simple RAG takes seconds. The slow part is asking a model for facts from every note.

items.text: A fact such as 'You --bring--> own cup' that no note supports
items.misconception: Simple RAG pastes the note's own words. Extracted facts are the model's reading of the text, so they can be wrong.

items.text: Raising k pastes more text into every prompt
items.misconception: The k setting belongs to simple retrieval. The graph walk has its own breadth setting, the number of hops.

questions.prompt: You switch the embedding model after building a LightRAG index. What does its documentation say you need to do?
questions.explain: Vectors from different embedding models are not comparable, and the docs say a change requires re-embedding the chunks, entities and relationships.

options.text: Re-embed the stored text, entities and relationships with the new model
Nothing, because all embedding models produce interchangeable vectors
options.misconception: Vectors from different models live in different spaces and often have different lengths. Mixing them gives meaningless similarity scores.

options.text: Raise the context length so the old vectors fit the new model
options.misconception: Context length limits how much text a model reads at once. It has no effect on whether old vectors match a new model.

options.text: Switch to a thinking model, which can adapt old vectors on the fly
options.misconception: Chat models do not rewrite stored vectors. The index has to be rebuilt with the model you will use at query time.

questions.prompt: A learner sets up LightRAG for the first time on a shared lab workstation. Which line of their plan is the risky one?
questions.explain: The docs say lightrag-server binds to all network interfaces with authentication off by default, so on a shared machine anyone who can reach the port could use it. Setting HOST=127.0.0.1 keeps it local.

lines.text: 1. Index a folder of ten mock notes first and read the extracted facts.
lines.why: A tiny mock folder is a safe way to see what extraction produces.

lines.text: 2. Start lightrag-server with its default settings and leave it running.
3. Set the context length to 32768 and use a non-thinking model for extraction.
lines.why: These follow the project's own requirements for Ollama.

lines.text: 4. Pick the embedding model before indexing and keep it.
lines.why: Changing it later means re-embedding everything.

questions.prompt: You ran graph.py once with one model on one question and it answered correctly. What can you conclude?
questions.explain: One run shows how the pieces fit together. It says nothing about how often the method works or how it compares on other questions.

options.text: The pieces fit together; test more questions before trusting it
Graph RAG is more accurate than simple RAG on every question
options.misconception: Simple RAG also answered correctly at k=5 and with all notes. One question cannot rank the methods.

options.text: The extracted facts must all be correct, since the answer was right
options.misconception: A right answer can sit beside wrong facts. The exercise's graph contained a fact about bringing a cup that no lab note supports.

options.text: Any smaller model will give exactly the same result
options.misconception: Extraction is harder for small models, and the tools' docs warn about malformed JSON. Read the triples whenever you change the model.

questions.prompt: Match each setting or file to its job.
questions.explain: Each piece sits at a different point in the pipeline: asking for JSON, embedding, limiting the walk and giving the model room to read.

pairs.left: The `format` field with a JSON schema
pairs.right: Makes the model reply with facts in a fixed shape
pairs.misconception: The schema controls the shape of the reply. It does not choose which notes are retrieved.

pairs.right: Turns notes and questions into vectors
pairs.misconception: The embed call returns vectors only. It does not write answers.

pairs.right: How far the walk follows links from the starting entities
pairs.misconception: Hops count steps along graph edges. The number of notes retrieved in simple RAG is k.

pairs.right: How much text the model can read at once
pairs.misconception: Context length sets the size of the window. Which entities are found is decided by the graph step.
